title: Chet
hook: with yud it spells chai, life

segments.voice: Yesterday, two words for the Sabbath, remember and keep, spoken as one. Your line was zayin remembers. What did you remember on purpose, and who did you tell? Today, a letter you may have already heard at a party. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-six.

The speeches are over. Somebody's uncle has talked a little too long, the bride's friend has made everyone cry, and now the glasses go up. Wine, whiskey, sparkling water, whatever's in hand. And the whole table says one word together: l'chaim! Glasses touch. People drink. At Jewish weddings, at a bris, at a new job, at a reunion, even after a funeral when the family sits down to eat, that's the word. It means to life. And the word for life starts with a sound you make from the back of your throat. That sound is today's letter.

Chet. Here's the letter, one step at a time. Start with its look. Chet is a cousin of heh, the breath letter from a few days ago. Heh has a small gap at the top left, as if air can still slip out. Chet closes that gap: two legs and a roof, sealed. And the sound changes with it. Not an easy h, but a breath pushed against the back of the throat, ch, like clearing it gently. Next, the word. Put chet beside a yud, a tiny hanging stroke, and you have chai: alive, living. Its plural, chayim, is the everyday word for life. L'chaim simply means to life. Then, a sentence that gives the word weight. Near the end of Deuteronomy, Moses stands before the people and lays out the choice in front of them. In the King James: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life." Not just enjoy it. Choose it, as if life were something you could keep picking up, day after day. Last, a custom. Tradition gives each Hebrew letter a number, and tradition says chet and yud together add up to eighteen. So some people give gifts in multiples of eighteen, and some wear the word chai on a chain around their neck. A number that means life. And l'chaim isn't only for weddings. You can say it over a cup of coffee with a friend you haven't seen in a while. It's a way of noticing, out loud, that you're both still here.
screen: `HEH WITH THE GAP CLOSED.` · `CHET AND YUD: CHAI, ALIVE.` · `THEREFORE CHOOSE LIFE.` · `EIGHTEEN, TRADITION SAYS.` · then, large: `L'CHAIM: TO LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a quiet toast to life. Settle, and breathe. If there's a cup or a glass near you, water, tea, anything, hold it. If not, just hold your hands as if there were. Bring to mind one thing in your life that's alive right now: a person, a friendship, a plant on the windowsill, a project that's finally growing. Lift the cup a little toward it, and say the word under your breath: l'chaim. Then sip, slowly, and let the thing you named stay with you. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. The bell holds the time.
Chet. The throaty letter that, with a yud beside it, spells chai: alive, life. Today's word.
Your line: chet for life. Today, raise a cup with someone, even just coffee, and say l'chaim. Then tell them what you're toasting. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: At Jewish celebrations, from weddings to a meal after a hard day, people raise a glass and say l'chaim, 'to life'; some give gifts in multiples of eighteen, the number tradition assigns to chai, and some wear the word chai as a pendant.

myth: chet and heh look completely different
they're cousins: heh has a small gap at the top left, chet closes it.
chayim is life; the toast is said at weddings and at other tables.
Moses says it in Deuteronomy: "therefore choose life."

fork.setup: you're Moses, near the end of the road, laying out life and death, blessing and curse before the people. what do you tell them?
options: life and death are out of your hands.
fork.reveal: "therefore choose life." the text treats life as something you choose, not only something that happens to you.

original.note: Hebrew: alive, living; chet (ח) plus yud (י). The toast l'chaim (לְחַיִּים) means to life.

trapdoor: what you thought: chet is just the throaty ch sound.
what it means: with yud it spells chai, alive, the life in l'chaim.
what a scholar hears: by the tradition of letter values, ח and י make eighteen, and Deuteronomy 30:19 makes life a choice: "therefore choose life."

sources.quoted: I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life

notes: Deuteronomy 30:19 quoted from the KJV (1769); JPS 1917 may read slightly differently. Confirm.
Gematria of chai (eighteen) and the custom of gifts in multiples of eighteen are given only as 'tradition says' / 'some people', per the claims rule; no text cited for it. Confirm acceptable.
Heh vs chet shapes: heh's left leg does not touch the roof, chet's does. Confirm description ('gap at the top left').
Hook lists occasions for l'chaim (weddings, a bris, a meal after a funeral) as narrative; confirm the funeral-meal example is appropriate.
'Near the end of Deuteronomy' and 'the end of the road' for Moses in Deuteronomy 30: confirm framing.

Editor: cut 'two syllables' (an uncited count, and l'chaim is often heard as three) and 'the smallest letter' for yud (tomorrow's superlative, uncited here); replaced the stock 'ordinary Tuesday' phrase.
